Method.groundingDescription: A sense of reality and being in the present moment
Method.groundingReadMore:
Before starting this exercise, pay attention to your breathing. Slow, deep, long breaths can help you maintain a sense of calm or help you return to a calmer state. Once you find your breath, go through the following steps to help ground yourself: 

5: Acknowledge FIVE things you see around you. It could be a pen, a spot on the ceiling, anything in your surroundings.

4: Acknowledge FOUR things you can touch around you. It could be your hair, a pillow, or the ground under your feet. 

3: Acknowledge THREE things you hear. This could be any external sound. If you can hear your belly rumbling that counts! Focus on things you can hear outside of your body.

2: Acknowledge TWO things you can smell. Maybe you are in your office and smell pencil, or maybe you are in your bedroom and smell a pillow. If you need to take a brief walk to find a scent you could smell soap in your bathroom, or nature outside.

1: Acknowledge ONE thing you can taste. What does the inside of your mouth taste like—gum, coffee, or the sandwich from lunch?

Method.breathingDescription: Controlling your breathing using a special technique

breathingTypes.prepare: Get into the position that's most comfortable for you, relax your shoulders, and click “Start.”
breathingTypes.boxDescription:
To begin box breathing, sit or stand with your back straight. Or, if you prefer, you can lie down with your arms by your side. Choose whatever position feels most relaxing.

      Close your eyes if it feels right for you.

      Take a moment to relax your shoulders, release any tension in your jaw and let your body settle. Then follow the steps below.

1. Breathe in slowly to a count of 4. If you want to, place your hands on your belly and feel it expand like a balloon.
2. After breathing in, hold your breath for another count of 4.
3. Breathe out slowly and steadily through your mouth, again counting to 4 in your mind.
4. After breathing out, hold your breath again for another count of 4.
5. Go back to step 1 and repeat the process for as long as you want to.
breathingTypes.478Description:
To begin 4-7-8 breathing, sit comfortably with a straight back. Or, if you’re using this exercise to help you fall asleep, lie down instead.

Throughout the session, your tongue should be resting gently against the roof of your mouth, just behind your top front teeth.

When you’re ready, follow the steps below.

1. Breathe in silently through your nose for a count of 4.
2. After breathing in, hold your breath for a count of 7.
3. Breathe out forcefully through your mouth for a count of 8, making a ‘whoosh’ sound as you let the air out. This may be easier if you purse your lips.
4. Go back to step 1 and repeat the process up to 3 more times, for a total of 4 rounds.

If you're a beginner, you might feel a bit lightheaded at first. This is normal. At first, you should only practice 4 rounds at a time. As you get used to the exercise, you can do it up to 8 times.

Method.videoDescription: Watching calming videos to shift your focus
Method.videoReadMore: Nature and meditation videos aren't just pretty to look at. Research shows they actually work: heart rate drops, the nervous system shifts into rest mode — that's real, measurable relaxation happening in your body. So if you feel calmer after watching — that's not in your head.
Method.interactiveReadMore:
Interactive exercises aren't just for fun. When you do something with your hands and see the result, your brain releases dopamine, stress drops, and you're left with that quiet sense of "done." Kind of like finishing a drawing or finally tidying up a shelf.
This works especially well if just "sitting and breathing" feels impossible — interactive tasks gently occupy your mind and leave less room for anxious thoughts.

interactiveSteps.touchScreenToStart: Touch the screen and swipe to draw

Method.creativeDescription: Suggestions for creative activities, such as crafts
Method.creativeReadMore:
Hands are a surprisingly powerful tool against anxiety. Crafting, gardening, playing an instrument — these aren't just hobbies. Research shows they genuinely lift your mood and make life feel more manageable.
When your hands are busy, your mind stops looping through anxious thoughts. And your body actually relaxes — the feel of soil or clay sends a signal to your nervous system: "we're okay, you can breathe now." It's one of the healthiest forms of distraction out there.

creativeSteps.knittingDescription: Try knitting a simple scarf or potholder. The rhythmic movements calm your nervous system.
creativeSteps.coloringDescription: Print a mandala pattern or grab an adult coloring book. Fill it with color without thinking about the result.
creativeSteps.claySculptingDescription: Grab some regular clay or plasticine. Make whatever you want — balls, snakes, abstract shapes.
creativeSteps.drawingDescription: Take a sheet of paper and draw what you see in front of you — a mug, your hand, the view from the window. No judgments.
creativeSteps.paperAirplanesDescription: Fold a few different paper airplanes. Focus on getting the folds just right, then send them flying.
creativeSteps.origamiDescription: Fold a simple figure: a frog, a boat, or a flower. All you need is a sheet of paper.
creativeSteps.plantCareDescription: Water and check on each plant at home. Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth. It's surprisingly meditative.
creativeSteps.herbPlantingDescription: Plant basil, dill, or parsley in a pot — seeds are available at any store.
creativeSteps.cookingDescription: Pick a recipe you've never tried before. Focus on the smells, textures, and the process itself.
creativeSteps.bakingDescription: Knead dough with your hands. The physical sensation of warm dough is calming in itself.
creativeSteps.collageDescription: Cut out words and images you like from old magazines and paste them onto a sheet of paper.
creativeSteps.embroideryDescription: Try simple embroidery: thread, a needle, a small piece of fabric. Start with a basic stem stitch.
creativeSteps.paperMosaicDescription: Tear colored paper into small pieces and arrange them into any picture on cardboard.
creativeSteps.woodworkDescription: Sand an old cutting board or wooden object. Smooth, steady hand movements make for great practice.
creativeSteps.watercolorDescription: Fill a glass with water, grab some watercolors, and just mix colors on paper. No plan needed.
creativeSteps.braceletWeavingDescription: Take some embroidery thread and weave a simple bracelet for yourself or a friend.
creativeSteps.sortingDescription: Go through a junk drawer, sort buttons by color or size. The monotony is surprisingly soothing.
creativeSteps.scrapbookingDescription: Put together a page from photos, tickets, and notes that have been sitting around doing nothing.
creativeSteps.snowflakesDescription: Fold a sheet of paper and cut out patterns with scissors. Every snowflake comes out unique.
creativeSteps.crochetDescription: Learn to make single crochet stitches — it's easier than knitting needles, and you'll see results fast.
creativeSteps.botanicalSketchDescription: Pick any plant or piece of fruit and draw it in pencil, trying to capture its shape and details.
creativeSteps.upcyclingDescription: Make something out of cardboard boxes, bottle caps, or jars. It doesn't have to be useful — that's fine.
creativeSteps.candlesDescription: Melt down old candle stubs, add essential oil, and pour into a glass. Simple and satisfying.
creativeSteps.restorationDescription: Take an old item — shoes, a bag, a picture frame — and tidy it up. Hands busy, mind at rest.
creativeSteps.dotDrawingDescription: Draw dots on paper and connect them into any pattern you like. No rules.
creativeSteps.newspaperWeavingDescription: Roll newspaper into tubes and weave a simple basket or trivet.
creativeSteps.stoneDecoratingDescription: Pick up a few stones outside and paint them with acrylics or markers.
creativeSteps.marblingDescription: Drop nail polish onto water and dip a sheet of paper in — you'll get a unique pattern every time.
creativeSteps.fingerKnittingDescription: No needles needed — you can weave yarn right on your fingers. Make a simple chain or a small mat.
creativeSteps.doodlingDescription: Fill a sheet of paper with patterns, swirls, grids, and waves. No goal — just let your hand move.

Method.pmrDescription: Techniques for physically relaxing the body
Method.pmrReadMore:
Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) is an actively engaging relaxation technique developed by Edmund Jacobson in the 1920s. PMR involves participants actively contracting muscles to create tension and progressively releasing this. The routine is repeated until participants acquire complete relaxation.

This technique utilizes the principles of neuronal “top-down” and “bottom-up” processing to achieve results. In “top-down” processing, participants use areas higher in the nervous system like the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum to contract muscles and gradually release the tension.

In “bottom-up” processing, the holding and releasing of bodily tension produce proprioceptive stimulation from peripheral muscles that ascends to the brain via the spinal cord and the brainstem. With both stimulatory passages activated, PMR provides participants with quick and immediate relief.

pmrSteps.startDescription: Find a comfortable position, release your shoulders, and take a few calm breaths. Start when you are ready.
pmrSteps.startImageAlt: Starting position for progressive muscle relaxation

forehead.title: Forehead
forehead.tenseDescription: Gently raise your eyebrows and tense your forehead. Hold the tension without pain.
forehead.relaxDescription: Release your forehead. Notice your face becoming smoother and calmer.

eyesNose.title: Eyes and nose
eyesNose.tenseDescription: Lightly squeeze your eyes shut and wrinkle your nose. Keep the tension gentle.
eyesNose.relaxDescription: Relax your eyes, bridge of the nose, and nose. Let your face soften.

lips.title: Lips
lips.tenseDescription: Press your lips together or gently push them forward. Hold the tension.
lips.relaxDescription: Release your lips and jaw. Let your mouth and chin relax.

shoulders.title: Shoulders
shoulders.tenseDescription: Lift your shoulders toward your ears and notice tension in your neck and shoulders.
shoulders.relaxDescription: Drop your shoulders down. Notice heaviness and warmth in your upper body.

back.title: Back
back.tenseDescription: Gently draw your shoulder blades together and lightly tense your back.
back.relaxDescription: Release your back. Let your shoulder blades and spine return to a comfortable position.

arms.title: Arms
arms.tenseDescription: Tense your arms from shoulders to forearms. Hold the effort steadily.
arms.relaxDescription: Relax your arms. Notice the tension moving down and away.

hands.title: Hands
hands.tenseDescription: Clench your hands into fists. Notice the tension in your palms and fingers.
hands.relaxDescription: Open your hands. Let your fingers rest freely.

belly.title: Belly
belly.tenseDescription: Gently tighten your belly muscles without holding your breath.
belly.relaxDescription: Release your belly. Breathe calmly and notice the soft movement of your breath.

legs.title: Legs
legs.tenseDescription: Tense your thighs and calves. Keep your feet steady and avoid pain.
legs.relaxDescription: Relax your legs. Notice support and heaviness in your thighs and calves.

toes.title: Toes
toes.tenseDescription: Curl or stretch your toes to create light tension.
toes.relaxDescription: Release your toes. Let your feet fully relax.

finalStep.M: Take a moment to just be here — and choose next step whenever you're ready.
finalStep.F: Take a moment to just be here — and choose next step whenever you're ready.

why.title: What this project is for
why.paragraph1: Anxiety affects everyone differently: it can freeze you, send you into panic, make it hard to focus, or even trigger different physical symptoms. Learning to cope with it is a long process of working with a specialist.
why.paragraph2: But in an anxious moment, it is important to help yourself calm down and gather your strength.
why.paragraph3: Be Capy was created to help you stop for a few minutes, breathe out, and feel a little better.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.description: What data Be Capy uses, why cookies are needed, and what rights users may have.

sections.title: In short
body: Be Capy aims to collect as little data as possible. At this stage, the site uses technical data needed to operate and a cookie that stores the selected interface language.
We do not ask users to enter their name, medical information, diagnoses, or other sensitive data.

sections.title: Data that may be processed
body: Technical data: IP address, browser type, device, requested URL, and request time may be processed by hosting and server infrastructure to display the site, maintain security, and diagnose errors.
The `locale` cookie: used to remember the selected interface language. This is a functional site preference.
Exercise or check-in data, if stored only in the user’s browser, is not sent to us as personal data unless server storage or accounts are added later.

sections.title: Purposes
body: Displaying the site and its features.
Saving the language preference.
Maintaining security, fixing errors, and improving stability.
Analytics may be added later only after this policy is updated and, where required, a consent mechanism is provided.

sections.title: Cookies and analytics
body: The site currently uses a functional language cookie. This cookie supports expected interface behavior.
If analytics, advertising, or third-party cookies are added later, users will receive information about them and, where required by law, a way to give or withdraw consent.
Embedded third-party services, such as YouTube videos, may set their own cookies and process data under their own terms when users interact with that content.

sections.title: Retention
body: The language cookie is stored for as long as needed to preserve the preference or until the user deletes cookies in the browser.
Server technical logs, if kept by hosting providers, are retained for the period needed for security, diagnostics, and service operation.

sections.title: Your rights
body: Depending on applicable law, you may have rights to request access, rectification, deletion, restriction, portability, or objection to processing.
For privacy requests, contact us at hello@uspokapi.ru.

sections.title: Changes
body: We may update this policy if site features change, including analytics, accounts, contact forms, or other data processing.

The materials are for general wellbeing and are not individual advice.

sections.title: Medical disclaimer
body: Be Capy does not replace medical, psychological, or psychiatric help.
The site is not intended to diagnose, treat, prevent, or cure any condition or to make health decisions.
If you have symptoms, a diagnosis, severe anxiety, panic attacks, depression, thoughts of self-harm, or any worsening condition, contact a qualified professional.

sections.title: Emergencies

sections.title: User responsibility
body: You decide whether an exercise is suitable for you. Stop an exercise if it causes discomfort, worsening symptoms, dizziness, pain, or other unpleasant sensations.
